items_missed: Save Your Ass speech: completely absent — 0/10. No mention that prep before move day shortens the move and lowers the bill, no consolidation examples (loose drawer items, photos off walls, kids' toys, garden tools), no 'take a carload' tip, no sense-check close. This was the single most wasted opportunity on the call: the customer volunteered the exact opening himself — 'it's probably gonna be less than that cause, you know I'm gonna be taking some stuff over' — and Dustin answered 'Okay. Okay.' He was already carloading things over and never got told that doing more of it, and consolidating the loose stuff before the crew arrives, is what keeps an hourly bill down.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — on a move whose defining item is a piano being delivered to a third party at a separate address. The customer even pre-qualified the risk conversation ('our furniture is nice but it wouldn't fall into any of those classification'), and the $2,000 repair/replace/reimburse promise was never said out loud.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned. This was the highest-value differentiator to skip on this specific call — the person being moved is an elderly woman entering assisted living and the son is coordinating remotely. A mover photo and bio emailed a few days out is exactly the reassurance that buyer wants.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned. He gave arrival mechanics instead — '8:30 and 9:00 just kinda depends on traffic' and a thirty-minute heads-up call — and then let a two-hour afternoon window sit there ('between 1:00 and 3:00') with no guarantee attached to either.

Clock start never explained: no 'the clock starts on-site when we open the contract.' The 2.5-hour minimum and quarter-hour proration were both covered well, but the customer was never told when the meter actually begins — and on a three-address job with 35-40 minutes of inter-stop driving, that is a live billing question he now has to guess at.

No sense-check anywhere in the call. 'Does that make sense?' or an equivalent appears zero times across a dense pricing, clock, and estimate block that ran several minutes with the customer reduced to 'Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.'

No deposit required — never said. A key Einstein differentiator, omitted at the exact moment it lands hardest: the customer had just agreed to lock the last truck ('Yeah, let's go ahead and do that now') and was never told there was nothing to pay to hold it.

Email handoff explained but underspecified: 'I'll have this confirmation email landing in your inbox' with no BOLDED-details framing at the top and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. The close routed questions forward ('You're welcome to reply to that email or give us a call here') rather than asking the customer to verify the details — which matters here because Dustin entered fabricated placeholder data ('I'm gonna put a thousand square feet and I have to have something in that field, I'm gonna call it a three bedroom house') and estimated the destination walk himself when the customer couldn't ('I have a feeling the kind of fifty yards to like, I don't know maybe thirty yards').
Hours and how to reach us: 'give us a call here' with no hours and no number.

Customer's name used zero times. He got it in the first ten seconds — 'my name's Kenneth Wilson' — and never said 'Kenneth' once in fifteen minutes. The cost showed up in the customer's own sign-off: 'Excellent, Justin. Thank you so much man.' Fifteen minutes and the customer still had the rep's name wrong, because names were never part of the conversation in either direction.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up. Opened straight into 'I was calling in regards to the quote request that you sent through our website.'

Agenda statement given but incomplete — 'we'll run through some quick details and then I can get you set up with an estimate and then onto a a truck if you're feeling good about it' names the sequence but never sets the 10-15 minute timeframe, and 'if you're feeling good about it' is a conditional, not the explicit 'Sound good?' confirmation.

Origin stairs/floors never established. He carefully confirmed the piano was going to a ground floor and that the destination unit was second-floor-with-elevator, but never asked whether the bed and dressers coming out of the 1,850 sq ft four-bedroom home are upstairs or down. On a two-person crew that is a material time variable.
Additional rooms never asked — no garage, attic, storage-unit, patio, or balcony question at a four-bedroom home being cleared out.

Packing needs never established. He landed on '25 boxes' as the planning number and never asked who is packing them or whether they want packing service — which also means he can't legitimately treat packing pricing as not-applicable; he never found out whether it applied. Related: 25 boxes were needed and no Ecobox referral was offered.

Moving-stressor question never asked — no 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?' Dustin came close and then stopped short: he showed real insight with 'a lot of times people moving into the assisted livings are sentimental about items that they've collected over the year,' which is precisely the moment to ask the worry question on a move-a-parent-into-care job, and he moved straight to the piano address instead.

Insurance explained only as a throwaway inclusion — '$192... is gonna cover the taxes the insurance' — with no No Worries framing and no 60c/lb baseline. Saying the rate covers 'the insurance' without explaining what that means is weaker than saying nothing, because the customer walks away thinking he is fully covered.

Estimate accuracy: the range floor is not credible. The quote was framed as landing 'between our two and a half hour minimum up to four hours,' $620-$908, then reinforced with 'I do think you're gonna land somewhere in between those two numbers.' Two movers cannot load a one-bedroom load plus 25 boxes, move an upright piano at a second address, drive 35-40 minutes across three stops, and carry everything ~30 yards to a second-floor elevator unit in 2.5 hours. The honest range starts at 3.5 and tops out above 4.
top_strength: The discovery and the estimate build were genuinely excellent — this is the best probe work in the batch, and it is worth banking as a teaching example. Dustin caught the trap in his own system: the quote form said four-bedroom, but the customer explained she was 'going from 1800 and, and fifty square feet down to like, 539,' and instead of quoting the form Dustin re-priced the actual load out loud, on the record: 'This move is a little other than typical, obviously, she's moving out of a four bedroom home that usually would take three to four guys. Six to eight hours. In this case I think the appropriate team size is a two person team.' That is exactly the manual override the estimate-accuracy rock is trying to produce. He then built the estimate from real variables rather than assumptions — he qualified the piano ('it's just a basic up, right. It's not like a grand or baby grand'), confirmed it was going to a ground floor, captured the third address, marked the stop ('let me mark drop-off piano there'), and validated both drive legs with the customer ('does it sound right that it's about twenty to 25 minutes from the Oana drive address?'). Two probes stand out. First, the box count, where he gave the customer an anchor and his reasoning instead of an open question: 'normally... moving into an apartment that size would expect to move around 25 boxes. Do you think she'll be taken about 25 boxes with her?' — then explained the range and pre-absorbed the downside, 'obviously if it's less, that's definitely not an issue at all.' Second, the walk-distance probe, which almost nobody runs: 'sometimes it's a little bit of a longer than typical traverse from the truck up to the unit... Do you have a guess of how far her unit is from the loading dock?' When the customer didn't know, Dustin bounded it with an equivalent rather than dropping it, and the customer volunteered the answer he needed ('once you hit the second floor, she's not very far'). He also handled scheduling with real transparency — weekend lead times, discounted versus standard days, the honest 'if it were a Friday or a Saturday that would slightly increase that hourly rate' — and closed cleanly on the scarcity he had established earlier: 'you wanted to go ahead and get that locked in on that last truck we have.' The customer's own verdict is the proof: 'This was a lot easier than I thought it was gonna be.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix by a wide margin: Dustin has no Save Your Ass speech. Zero of ten, and the customer handed him the opening unprompted when he said 'I'm gonna be taking some stuff over to and so it'll probably be less than that.' The reply needed to be: 'Kenneth, that actually helps you twice — since this is hourly, every carload you take over yourself is time our guys don't spend, so the more you can consolidate before we get there the shorter the bill. Biggest wins are the loose stuff: empty out the dresser drawers into boxes, get the photos and frames off the walls, and box up anything small enough to hand-carry. Anything that fits in your car, take it. Does that make sense?' On a job priced at $192/hour where he is already forecasting the move runs past the minimum, that speech is the difference between a 3.5-hour move and a 4.5-hour one, and it is the same lever the estimate-accuracy rock is chasing from the other direction. Second priority: the three differentiators were all skipped on the call that needed them most. This is an elderly woman moving into assisted living, coordinated by her son, with a piano going to a third party — Meet Your Mover, No Worries, and the On-Time Guarantee are the whole reassurance package for a remote decision-maker, and none of them were spoken. Bundle them where the pricing was already landing: 'That rate includes our No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse any accidental damage, and I'm noting the piano on the job so the crew brings the board and straps. A few days before the move you'll get a Meet Your Mover email with a photo and a little background on the guys coming, so nobody's a stranger at the door. And we back the arrival window with an On-Time Guarantee — if we miss it, we start discounting immediately.' Third, and this one is a real business risk, not just a scorecard miss: Dustin quoted a floor of 2.5 hours on a three-address, two-mover, piano-plus-25-boxes job with 35-40 minutes of driving and a 30-yard elevator carry, and then reinforced the anchor with 'I do think you're gonna land somewhere in between those two numbers.' That range should have opened at 3.5, and the piano probably wants three movers rather than two, which also protects the crew. Quoting a floor nobody can hit is how a 52% estimate-accuracy number gets made, and it converts a delighted customer into a surprised invoice. Two smaller cleanups: say the customer's name — he had 'Kenneth' from second one and never used it, and the customer signed off calling him 'Justin,' which is what a fifteen-minute call with no names in it sounds like. And add the two missing close lines: 'There's no deposit — nothing to pay to hold the date,' and 'The top of that email has the key details in bold; give it a quick read and reply if anything's off.' That second one matters more than usual here, because Dustin entered placeholder data on the piano address ('I'm gonna put a thousand square feet... I'm gonna call it a three bedroom house') and estimated the destination walk distance himself, so the confirmation email is the only checkpoint where the customer can catch a wrong assumption before move day.
phone_presence_notes: High, genuine energy throughout with constant natural affirmations ('Absolutely,' 'Beautiful beautiful, awesome,' 'Okay, no, that's no problem'), real empathy for the assisted-living context ('a lot of times people moving into the assisted livings are sentimental about items that they've collected over the year'), and a customer who ended visibly relieved — 'This was a lot easier than I thought it was gonna be' — held back only by never once using the customer's name, which is likely why the customer closed by calling him 'Justin.'
